en: O best of ascetics, do you wish to cast away the fivefold intellect from the food-sheath to the food-sheath, or consciousness from consciousness? Speak! Go, go!
In the ocean of consciousness—the inward reality, the waveless sea of innate bliss—what great delusion of duality is this that says "this is a Brahmin" or "this is an outcaste"?
Is there any difference between the sun reflected in the waters of the Ganges and the water in the gutter of a *cāṇḍāla*, or between a golden pitcher and a clay pot in the sky?

That consciousness which manifests most clearly throughout waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; which is woven through the bodies of all beings from Brahma down to a tiny ant; and which is the witness of the universe—that alone am I, and not the visible objects.
If one possesses such firm wisdom, then whether he be an outcaste or a twice-born, he is my teacher; this is my conviction. 1.
"I am indeed Brahman, and this entire universe is an expansion of pure consciousness; all this has been fashioned by me through the threefold ignorance.
He whose mind is firmly established in this way in the supremely blissful, eternal, and stainless Supreme—whether he be an outcaste or a twice-born, he is, in my view, a Guru. (2)

Having ascertained that the entire universe is eternally impermanent, constantly contemplating the eternal Brahman through the words of my Guru with an unfeignedly peaceful mind, and burning away all past and present evil deeds in the fire of pure consciousness, I have offered my own body to the force of *prārabdha*—this is my resolve. (3)
That which is clearly grasped within as "I" by animals, humans, and gods; by whose light the heart, senses, body, and objects—which are themselves insentient—shine forth;
that manifestation, resembling the orb of the sun obscured by clouds, the yogi who constantly contemplates with a tranquil mind is indeed a Guru: such is my conviction. (4)

That which is but a tiny fraction of a fraction of the ocean of bliss by which these Śakras and others are satisfied; that state of mind in which the Sage, having attained utter tranquility of thought, is liberated;

that ocean of eternal bliss in which one whose intellect has dissolved becomes Brahman itself and no longer a knower of Brahman—he whose feet are worshipped by the lords of the gods is surely my ideal. (5)
"O Śambhu, from the perspective of the body I am your servant; O Three-eyed One, from the perspective of the individual soul (jīva) I am born as a portion of you;
and from the perspective of the Self, O Soul of all, you alone are I—such is my conviction, established by all the scriptures."
Thus ends "The Five Verses of Wisdom" (Manīṣāpañcaka), composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat.
